title: How many decision makers are we talking about?
html:
A few weeks ago, I had the pleasure to attend the 2015 Information Systems for Crisis Response and Management (ISCRAM) conference in Norway, where several sessions focused on decision makers. To help structure part of the discussion and ensure that we were moving forward, we leveraged the Humanitarian Decision Makers Taxonomy.

At one point, a question was raised “How many decision makers are we talking about?”. This is a question I had asked myself after responding to Typhoon Haiyan.

Late last year, I collaborated with Monique Yamgouet Ndam to try to figure out just how many different decision-maker roles exist during an emergency and how many decision makers exist within each of the taxonomy branches. We decided to use Typhoon Haiyan as a case study as it was the most recent large-scale and open emergency. Because I had responded to Haiyan, I was able to provide guidance to the research and interpretation of the results.  

One of the first challenges Monique encountered was the absence of clear-cut lines between some of the taxonomy branches. Individuals spilled over into other branches like NGOs, Public Sector or International Organizations as time went on, for example. But, she persevered. She spent hours scanning through sources such as UN and NGO reports (situation reports, response reports, appeals, etc.), military reports, donation announcements, the UN Business Brief, reports by Chamber of Commerces in the Philippines, media news reports, assessment reports such as the Multi-Cluster Initial Rapid Assessment, government reports, UNDAC’s End of Mission Report, responder check-ins on HumanitarianResponse.info, ReliefWeb material, general coordination calls, and (internal) OCHA Task Force meetings. She even leveraged sources like the 144 citations on the Humanitarian Response to Typhoon Haiyan Wikipedia Page. When a classification challenge arose, we sought guidance from deployed OCHA Field Information Services team members and/or contacted the OHCA Philippines office.

Here is the result of Monique’s work.

(Note that, for illustration purposes, a minimum and maximum bubble size was determined. In some cases, bubble size is not proportionate to the data.)

Download animated GIF | Download PDF [2.5 MB]

When I showed this animated GIF at ISCRAM, the first reaction was “Wow!”, quickly followed by “Where did you get the data?!”. The GIF helped to frame portions of a discussion about which decision maker groups could be studied, what scale would be required, and potential ideas on how it could be done.

Hopefully this animated taxonomy can help to structure and guide other fruitful discussions.

Andrej

FYI: The data that we compiled is not derived from official numbers of decision makers and is only used here for illustrative purposes.
teaser: Estimating the number of humanitarian decision makers with an animated taxonomy; the figures are illustrative, not official.
